title: Looking for material about the production of 90s Japanese independent films

commenti.body:
I think the best place to look to will be books. A few suggestions with the caveat that I'm not sure if they are exactly what you're looking for:

* *Japanese Film and the Challenge of Video*, Tom Mes (quite new still so a bit pricey)
   * This book champions V-Cinema, why it's been overlooked, and why it shouldn't be.
* *Contemporary Japanese Film*, Mark Schilling
   * A majority of this book is profiles on/interviews with various directors that you may love, but the beginning has some good insights that I think may be what you are looking for.
* *The Midnight Eye Guide to New Japanese Film*, Tom Mes and Jasper Sharp
   * As with *Contemporary Japanese Film*, this book is largely profiles on directors and a selection of their films. This may be worth looking into if enough of the covered directors are of interest to you.

There is a great making-of on the *Tampopo* Blu-ray released by Criterion, it's feature length and made by Juzo Itami himself. This is, of course, not a 90s film but I did find it to be fascinating since he covers almost every aspect of making this film and it's extra useful since he is the director and not a 3rd party observer.

Really looking forward to get my hands on the new Tom Mes book! I love the Midnight Eye crew, currently going through The Midnight Eye Guide to New Japanese Film after finishing Behind the Pink Curtain, which are both more than 15 years old, so something that covers the '90s period onwards will be very interesting to get into.

The book by Adam Bingham, ***Contemporary Japanese Cinema Since Hana-Bi*** (2015) covers in its introduction what he thinks makes the Japanese 90s cinema so special, then develops more detail from Kitano's Hana-Bi onwards (1997).

Not strictly a 90s film, but close enough, is Tsukamoto's frenzied indie film ***Tetsuo The Iron Man*** (1989) which is my favourite from this period. It's very much like Lynch's ***Eraserhead*** but where Lynch goes squishy, Tsukamoto goes clangy. The 1992 sequel ***Tetsuo 2 Body Hammer*** is squarely in your time period though. 

Kiyoshi Kurosawa's ***Cure*** (1997) is not his first feature but the first with some recognition and generally seen as his first mature work. **Bong Joon-Ho** rates it as **the best film ever made**, which is quite the accolade.
